messages.content: I want to learn reduced models of partially observed Kuramoto–Sivashinsky dynamics. The goal is to preserve the stationary energy distribution and predict how mean energy responds to unseen forcing.

That sets two distinct requirements for the reduced models. Their stationary energy distributions should closely match the full-system distribution, and they should predict nonzero mean-energy responses to unseen weak forcing when compared with full-system simulations.
The distribution target is specific: its Wasserstein-1 error must stay below 5% of the full-system energy distribution’s standard deviation.

Understood. If the Wasserstein-1 distance between a reduced model’s stationary energy distribution and the full-system stationary energy distribution is denoted by W₁, and the standard deviation of the full-system distribution by σ_full, the requirement is W₁ < 0.05 σ_full. The 5% is relative to that standard deviation, not to the mean energy.
Why specify the standard deviation in the comparison?

It gives the distributional error a scale tied to the spread of the full-system energy distribution. Wasserstein-1 distance has the same units as energy here, so comparing it with 5% of that distribution’s standard deviation is dimensionally meaningful. The stated requirement does not supply a numerical value for the standard deviation or for the permitted Wasserstein-1 distance.
Would matching the stationary mean energy alone establish the distribution requirement?

No. The requirement concerns the stationary energy distribution as a distribution, measured by Wasserstein-1 distance. Agreement in a single summary such as mean energy does not, by itself, establish that its Wasserstein-1 distance from the full-system distribution is below the specified threshold.
The forcing target is separate: nonzero mean-energy responses to unseen weak forcing should be predicted within 10% relative error against full-system simulations.

Yes. For a nonzero mean-energy response from a full-system simulation, the reduced model’s predicted response should differ from it by no more than 10% relative to the full-system response. The forcing is described as weak and unseen; the requirement does not specify particular forcing signals or a training procedure.
Could you spell out what the relative-error comparison uses as its reference?

The reference is the response obtained from the full-system simulation. If R_full is that nonzero mean-energy response and R_reduced is the reduced model’s prediction of it, the stated target can be written as |R_reduced − R_full| / |R_full| ≤ 0.10. The nonzero condition matters because a relative error with |R_full| in the denominator would otherwise be undefined.
Does ‘nonzero’ describe the weak forcing or the energy response?

In this requirement, ‘nonzero’ describes the mean-energy response being predicted. ‘Weak’ describes the unseen forcing. Those are different qualifications: the response target concerns cases with a nonzero full-system response to unseen weak forcing.
If a reduced model meets the stationary distribution threshold, can I infer that it meets the response threshold too?

Not from these requirements alone. One assesses closeness of stationary energy distributions using Wasserstein-1 distance; the other assesses predictions of nonzero mean-energy responses to unseen weak forcing using relative error against full-system simulations. Satisfying either numerical condition does not, on its own, establish the other.
And does the response requirement replace the distribution requirement when forcing is involved?

No. They are both parts of the goal. The distribution condition remains a Wasserstein-1 error below 5% of the full-system distribution’s standard deviation, while the response condition remains prediction of nonzero mean-energy responses to unseen weak forcing within 10% relative error against full-system simulations. The wording does not specify an additional distributional threshold under forcing.
Does ‘partially observed’ tell us which quantities are available to the reduced model?

It says the dynamics are partially observed, but it does not identify the observed quantities or specify an observation scheme. It would go beyond the stated goal to assume, for example, that energy is the only observation or that particular state variables are available.
Nor have we settled on a particular form of reduced model, correct?

Correct. The goal is to learn reduced models with the stated distributional and response properties. It does not prescribe an architecture, a reduction method, a model size, or an estimation procedure.
I also want to avoid treating this as a reported success. How should it be phrased?

Phrase the numerical conditions as targets, not measured outcomes: learn reduced models of partially observed Kuramoto–Sivashinsky dynamics whose stationary energy-distribution Wasserstein-1 error stays below 5% of the full-system distribution’s standard deviation, and whose predictions of nonzero mean-energy responses to unseen weak forcing are within 10% relative error of full-system simulations. Nothing in the goal says those targets have already been achieved.

For that goal, I propose fitting a history-encoded stochastic latent SDE conditioned on forcing projections. I’d regularize it with an energy-distribution Wasserstein loss and weak-force response kernels.

That is a proposed way to connect the partially observed dynamics to both parts of the goal. A history encoder would represent information from past observations in a latent state, and a stochastic latent SDE would describe that state’s evolution while conditioning on projections of the forcing. The two regularizers would address different properties: the energy-distribution Wasserstein loss concerns stationary energy statistics, while the weak-force response kernels concern responses to weak forcing. This is a fitting proposal, not a claim that the accuracy targets have been met.
Why use a history-encoded state rather than describe it simply as a latent SDE?

The history-encoded qualifier matters because the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky dynamics are only partially observed in the goal. It indicates that the latent representation is informed by an observation history, rather than being identified with a fully observed instantaneous state. The proposal does not specify which observations are available, how far back the history extends, or how the encoder is built.
And what does ‘stochastic’ commit us to here?

It commits the proposed latent dynamics to an SDE—a stochastic differential equation—rather than describing them solely by deterministic latent evolution. It does not specify the drift, the stochastic term, their functional forms, or a reason that any particular source of uncertainty dominates.
I said the model is conditioned on forcing projections. Is that the same as specifying the forcing representation?

No. Conditioning on forcing projections says that projected information about the forcing enters the proposed latent dynamics. It does not identify the projections, their dimension, or how they are obtained. Keeping that distinction matters when discussing predictions for unseen forcing: the proposal states what kind of conditioning is intended without yet specifying its implementation.
How does the Wasserstein regularizer relate to the stationary-distribution requirement?

It is meant to encourage agreement between stationary energy distributions. That aligns with the goal’s explicit comparison: the reduced model’s stationary energy-distribution Wasserstein-1 error should stay below 5% of the full-system distribution’s standard deviation. Including a Wasserstein loss in fitting is a way to aim at that property; it does not, by itself, demonstrate that the threshold is satisfied.
Should I say the loss directly enforces the 5% threshold?

I would not equate the two. The proposal specifies regularization by an energy-distribution Wasserstein loss, whereas the 5% figure is an accuracy requirement to assess against the full-system stationary energy distribution. A regularizer can encourage a property without guaranteeing a particular measured bound. The proposal also does not specify a loss weight or an enforcement rule.
What role do the weak-force response kernels play alongside that loss?

They provide a separate way to regularize behavior under weak forcing, rather than relying only on agreement of stationary energy distributions. Their intended connection is to the goal of predicting nonzero mean-energy responses to unseen weak forcing within 10% relative error against full-system simulations. The proposal does not give a formula for the kernels or state how they are estimated.
Does regularizing with response kernels mean we have already shown the model generalizes to unseen forcing?

No. Regularizing with weak-force response kernels is part of the proposed fit. Prediction on unseen weak forcing, with nonzero mean-energy responses compared against full-system simulations, is still the stated target. The proposal alone supplies no evaluation result.
Could matching the weak-force response kernels make the Wasserstein regularizer unnecessary?

That is not a conclusion established by the proposal. It includes both regularizers: an energy-distribution Wasserstein loss and weak-force response kernels. They are directed at related but distinct aspects of the goal, and the supplied information does not say that either can be dropped or that one guarantees the other’s target.
I want the proposal stated precisely without making it sound like a completed experiment.

Propose fitting a history-encoded stochastic latent SDE for the partially observed Kuramoto–Sivashinsky dynamics, conditioned on forcing projections and regularized by an energy-distribution Wasserstein loss and weak-force response kernels. The intended targets remain a stationary energy-distribution Wasserstein-1 error below 5% of the full-system distribution’s standard deviation and prediction of nonzero mean-energy responses to unseen weak forcing within 10% relative error against full-system simulations. This describes the proposed approach and its targets, not achieved results.
Are 16 observation snapshots sufficient for the latent SDE to capture hidden-mode memory driving mean-energy responses?

That remains an open question. Sixteen snapshots specify the length of an observation history, but the count alone does not establish whether it contains enough information about hidden-mode memory to predict mean-energy responses. It does not tell us how the snapshots are spaced, what time span they cover, or how informative the partial observations are about the relevant hidden dynamics.
What would it mean for the latent SDE to capture that memory?

In this context, it would mean that the history-encoded latent state retains enough information from past observations for the model’s subsequent evolution to reflect the influence of unobserved modes on mean-energy responses. That is a statement about the proposed model’s predictive behavior, not necessarily a claim that its latent variables identify individual physical hidden modes.
So the question is not simply whether an encoder can accept a sequence of length 16?

Right. Being able to encode 16 observation snapshots is different from those snapshots being sufficient. The substantive question is whether the resulting latent state represents the memory needed for the mean-energy response, despite only partial observation.
Would 16 snapshots necessarily correspond to a particular amount of past time?

No. Without their spacing, 16 snapshots do not specify a temporal window. Nor does the snapshot count tell us how that window compares with the duration over which hidden-mode effects might matter to the response.
If the latent SDE is conditioned on forcing projections, why might the observation history still matter?

The forcing projections and observation history serve different roles in the proposal. The projections provide information about forcing; the history encoder is intended to represent information about the partially observed dynamical state. Conditioning on forcing does not, by itself, establish that the model knows the hidden state or its relevant memory.
Does making the latent dynamics stochastic solve the hidden-memory issue?

Not automatically. A stochastic latent SDE can represent uncertain latent evolution, but stochasticity alone does not show that a state encoded from 16 snapshots retains the particular past-dependent information needed to predict mean-energy responses.
Could a model match the stationary energy distribution yet still leave this question unanswered?

Yes. The stationary energy-distribution target concerns Wasserstein-1 error below 5% of the full-system distribution’s standard deviation. The 16-snapshot question specifically concerns whether hidden-mode memory relevant to mean-energy responses is captured. Agreement on the stationary distribution would not, on its own, settle that response question.
Would regularizing with weak-force response kernels settle it?

The proposed kernel regularization is meant to encourage appropriate weak-force responses, but its inclusion is not evidence that 16 snapshots are sufficient. The question remains whether the fitted latent SDE can predict the relevant mean-energy responses, including the stated target for nonzero responses to unseen weak forcing: within 10% relative error against full-system simulations.
Is that 10% target a test of whether the model has recovered the hidden modes themselves?

It is a target for prediction of mean-energy responses, not a direct requirement to recover individual hidden modes. Meeting it would speak to response accuracy under the specified comparison; it would not, by itself, identify what the latent variables correspond to internally.
Then I should leave the 16-snapshot point as a question rather than an assertion?

Yes: ask whether 16 observation snapshots give the history-encoded latent SDE enough information to capture hidden-mode memory relevant to mean-energy responses. The supplied information does not establish either that 16 are sufficient or that they are insufficient.

Here is my hypothesis about the history length: 16 observation snapshots at 0.25-time-unit spacing capture the hidden-mode memory needed by the latent SDE, yielding less than 10% relative mean-energy response error under held-out weak forcing.

That is a specific, testable hypothesis, not an established result. It links a defined observation history—16 snapshots spaced 0.25 time units apart—to two claims: that the history captures hidden-mode memory relevant to the response, and that the resulting latent SDE predicts mean-energy responses under held-out weak forcing with relative error strictly below 10%.
How much time does that sequence span?

If the 16 snapshots are consecutive and each neighboring pair is 0.25 time units apart, there are 15 intervals from the first snapshot to the last. The elapsed time between them is therefore 15 × 0.25 = 3.75 time units. That calculation describes the observation window; it does not establish that the window covers all relevant hidden-mode memory.
Why distinguish 16 snapshots from 16 intervals?

Because the spacing applies between snapshots. Sixteen observation times have 15 gaps between the first and last, so multiplying 16 by 0.25 would not give their first-to-last separation. The hypothesis specifies both the number of snapshots and their spacing.
Does the hypothesis say the latent state actually identifies the hidden modes?

No. ‘Capture hidden-mode memory’ can mean that the history-encoded latent state retains information needed to predict how hidden dynamics affect mean-energy responses. It need not mean that individual hidden modes are directly observed or uniquely identified in the latent state. Whether the predictive claim holds is still to be determined.
What exactly is predicted to be below 10%?

The predicted quantity is the relative error in the mean-energy response under held-out weak forcing. In the setting of the stated goal, the comparison is to the mean-energy response from full-system simulations. For a nonzero full-system response, it can be expressed as |R_reduced − R_full| / |R_full| < 0.10. The strict ‘less than’ reflects the wording of this hypothesis.
Is ‘held-out’ important, or could the hypothesis be about forcing used in fitting?

‘Held-out’ is important here: the hypothesis concerns weak forcing not used for fitting in that comparison. An error below 10% on forcing already used in fitting would not, by itself, establish the stated prediction about held-out weak forcing.
Does the 0.25-time-unit spacing itself guarantee that hidden-mode memory is captured?

No. The spacing and snapshot count define the proposed history, while sufficiency is the hypothesis being tested. Those numbers alone do not show how much information the partial observations carry about hidden-mode effects on mean-energy responses.
Suppose the response prediction were accurate under held-out weak forcing. Would that prove the entire hidden dynamics had been reconstructed?

No. Accurate mean-energy response predictions would support the predictive part of the hypothesis for the assessed forcing, but would not by themselves show reconstruction of every hidden dynamical feature. The claim is about memory relevant to mean-energy responses, not complete recovery of the unobserved system.
How does this relate to the proposed stochastic latent SDE with forcing projections?

The 16 snapshots at 0.25-time-unit spacing would provide the observation history from which the proposed model encodes its latent state. That latent SDE is also proposed to be conditioned on forcing projections. The hypothesis is that this particular history provides enough information about hidden-mode memory for the model to achieve the stated response accuracy under held-out weak forcing; conditioning on forcing does not settle that question on its own.
And does this hypothesis also assert that the stationary energy-distribution target is met?

No. It addresses hidden-mode memory and mean-energy response error under held-out weak forcing. The separate stationary target remains a Wasserstein-1 error below 5% of the full-system energy distribution’s standard deviation; this hypothesis makes no claim that target has been achieved.
So I should not present the less-than-10% figure as a measurement yet?

Correct. Present it as the predicted outcome: 16 observation snapshots at 0.25-time-unit spacing are hypothesized to capture hidden-mode memory sufficiently for the latent SDE to attain less than 10% relative mean-energy response error under held-out weak forcing. No measured response error or validation result is stated here.

To examine whether 16 observation snapshots are enough for the latent SDE, I plan to train matched latent SDEs using 4, 16, or 64 snapshots. I’ll compare their held-out forcing response errors and stationary-energy Wasserstein distances.

That plan varies the number of observation snapshots while comparing the same two kinds of outcomes across the matched latent SDEs. Held-out forcing response errors address how well the models predict responses to forcing outside the fit; stationary-energy Wasserstein distances address how closely their stationary energy distributions resemble the full-system distribution. It is a planned comparison, not a report of trained models or measured errors.
Why include both 4 and 64 rather than just fit the 16-snapshot model?

They give the 16-snapshot result points of comparison at a shorter and a longer history length. Comparing 4, 16, and 64 snapshots could reveal whether the measured response errors or stationary-energy distances differ across those choices. The plan does not predict which choice will perform best.
What does ‘matched latent SDEs’ convey here?

It conveys an intention to make the models comparable so the snapshot-count comparison is meaningful. The plan does not specify the matching protocol or say which other model properties are held fixed, so I would not present any particular set of controls as already decided.
Does the plan fix the spacing between snapshots for all three models?
No. It specifies 4, 16, or 64 snapshots, but it does not specify their spacing or the elapsed time covered by each history. Those details cannot be inferred from the snapshot counts alone.
The earlier 16-snapshot hypothesis mentions 0.25-time-unit spacing. Should we assume that spacing also applies to this comparison?

The plan does not say so. The 0.25-time-unit spacing belongs to the stated 16-snapshot hypothesis; it is not specified as a common spacing for the 4-, 16-, and 64-snapshot models in this plan. We can identify the question the comparison addresses without silently adding that design choice.
Could a difference between models reflect the duration of the observation window rather than the number of observations?

That is a conceptual issue worth keeping in mind when interpreting such a comparison: snapshot count and elapsed window can depend on how observations are spaced. Because the plan supplies no spacing or window lengths, it does not establish how those factors would be separated.
What would the held-out forcing comparison tell us about hidden-mode memory?

It would compare the models’ response-prediction behavior when their encoded histories contain different numbers of observations. That is relevant to the question of whether a 16-snapshot history carries enough information about hidden-mode memory to predict mean-energy responses. Response error is an observable consequence to compare; it is not a direct measurement of individual hidden modes or proof of how a latent state represents them.
Should the response errors be described as mean-energy response errors?

Yes, to keep the comparison tied to the question and the goal: compare errors in predicting mean-energy responses under held-out forcing. For the stated accuracy target, the relevant cases are nonzero responses to unseen weak forcing, compared against full-system simulations. The plan itself does not give any response-error values.
And how does the stationary-energy comparison fit in?

It checks a different property of the same planned models. The stationary-energy Wasserstein distances compare their stationary energy distributions with the full-system stationary energy distribution. In the goal, the specific distributional criterion is a Wasserstein-1 error below 5% of the full-system distribution’s standard deviation. A response-error comparison alone would not answer that distributional question.
Are those Wasserstein distances and response errors interchangeable measures of performance?

No. They measure different discrepancies: one concerns stationary energy distributions, and the other concerns predicted mean-energy responses under held-out forcing. The plan calls for comparing both across the 4-, 16-, and 64-snapshot latent SDEs, without assuming that a model’s standing on one comparison determines its standing on the other.
Does the word ‘held-out’ mean the forcing responses have already been simulated?

No. Here it describes the intended response comparison using forcing held out from fitting. The plan does not state that the latent SDEs have been trained, that any held-out predictions have been made, or that response errors have been measured.
Can we say now that 16 snapshots are sufficient because they are in the middle of the three choices?

No. Its position between 4 and 64 is just a feature of the proposed comparison. Whether 16 snapshots suffice to capture memory relevant to mean-energy responses cannot be determined from the selected counts; that is what the planned response-error comparison is meant to investigate.
Could the stationary-energy distances settle that sufficiency question by themselves?

Not by themselves. A small stationary-energy Wasserstein distance would concern the distribution of energy in stationary behavior. The sufficiency question asks whether the encoded history captures hidden-mode memory relevant to mean-energy responses, so the held-out forcing response errors are also needed for the planned comparison.
Please restate the plan without suggesting any result or adding experimental details.

Train matched latent SDEs using 4, 16, or 64 observation snapshots, then compare their held-out forcing response errors and stationary-energy Wasserstein distances. The comparison is intended to examine the role of observation-history length in predicting mean-energy responses while also tracking agreement with stationary energy distributions; no outcome is specified.
The activity is to fit 4-, 16-, and 64-snapshot latent SDEs on eight observed Kuramoto–Sivashinsky Fourier modes, then measure normalized energy W1 and held-out forcing-response errors.

That makes the observation setting more specific: the latent SDEs use histories of eight observed KS Fourier modes, with histories containing 4, 16, or 64 snapshots. The measurements are normalized energy Wasserstein-1 distance and errors in responses to held-out forcing. The activity describes what to fit and measure; it does not state any measured values.
What does ‘eight observed KS Fourier modes’ tell us about partial observation?

It identifies the observations used for this activity as eight Fourier modes of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky dynamics. It does not say that the full dynamical state is observed, identify which eight modes they are, or specify how any unobserved modes are represented by the latent SDE.
Does a 16-snapshot history mean 16 observations of each of those eight modes?

It means the 16-snapshot model uses a history of 16 observations of the specified eight-mode observation set. The activity does not give the snapshots’ timing or the format in which the Fourier-mode observations are supplied to the model.
Can we infer the elapsed time covered by the 4-, 16-, and 64-snapshot histories?
No. Snapshot counts alone do not determine elapsed time. This activity does not specify spacing, so it does not establish the duration of any of the three histories.
There was a hypothesis about 16 snapshots at 0.25-time-unit spacing. Is that spacing part of this activity?

It is not stated in this activity. Here the specified history lengths are 4, 16, and 64 snapshots, and the observation set is eight KS Fourier modes. The activity supplies no snapshot spacing for any of the three fits.
What does the ‘energy W1’ measurement compare?

In the context of the stationary-energy goal, it concerns Wasserstein-1 distance between a latent model’s stationary energy distribution and the full-system stationary energy distribution. It is a distributional comparison, not merely a comparison of mean energies.
And what does ‘normalized’ add?

It indicates that the energy Wasserstein-1 distance is to be reported on a normalized scale. This activity does not specify the normalization factor, so I would not assign one as a fact. If it is normalized by the full-system energy distribution’s standard deviation, the goal’s Wasserstein-1 threshold would read as a normalized value below 0.05; that is a conditional interpretation, not a specified calculation in this activity.
So should we report normalized energy W1 as if the denominator is already fixed?

No. We can say that normalized energy W1 is to be measured, but the stated activity does not define its denominator. The goal separately specifies the comparison of unnormalized stationary energy-distribution W1 with 5% of the full-system distribution’s standard deviation.
What are the held-out forcing-response errors meant to assess?

They assess how well the fitted latent SDEs predict responses to forcing held out from fitting. For the broader goal, the particular accuracy target concerns nonzero mean-energy responses to unseen weak forcing, with relative error assessed against full-system simulations. This activity calls for measuring held-out forcing-response errors but does not give their values or define any additional forcing cases.
Does the activity specify the exact formula for those response errors?

No. It names held-out forcing-response errors without defining an error formula. The goal does specify a relative-error target for nonzero mean-energy responses: the prediction should be within 10% relative error against full-system simulations. We should not assume this activity has supplied further conventions for calculating or aggregating the errors.
Why measure both energy W1 and forcing-response errors for every history length?

They address the two properties sought from the reduced model. Energy W1 addresses agreement of stationary energy distributions; forcing-response errors address predictive behavior under held-out forcing. Comparing both for 4-, 16-, and 64-snapshot latent SDEs keeps the history-length question connected to both properties without assuming that one measurement determines the other.
Would a low normalized energy W1 prove that eight observed modes retain enough hidden-mode memory?

Not by itself. A low energy W1 would indicate closeness on the measured stationary energy-distribution comparison. Whether a history of eight observed modes contains enough information for mean-energy response prediction is a separate question that the held-out forcing-response errors help examine.
If the 64-snapshot model had the smallest response error, could we conclude that more snapshots always help?

No such result is given here, and even a comparison among these three history lengths would concern those fitted models and measured responses. It would not establish a general rule for every possible history length or observation setting.
Are the three latent SDEs already fitted according to this wording?

The wording identifies fitting the 4-, 16-, and 64-snapshot latent SDEs and measuring their errors as the activity. It supplies no completed fit, measured normalized W1, or held-out forcing-response result, so I would not present any of those as accomplished.
Can you give me a precise statement of the activity without adding choices about spacing or normalization?

Fit latent SDEs using histories of 4, 16, or 64 snapshots of eight observed Kuramoto–Sivashinsky Fourier modes. For those fits, measure normalized stationary-energy Wasserstein-1 distances and held-out forcing-response errors. The snapshot spacing, normalization convention, and measured outcomes are not specified.
The resulting artifact is KS-MemoryBench v1. It contains 4-, 16-, and 64-snapshot SDE checkpoints, held-out forcing trajectories, and tables of normalized energy-W1 and mean-response errors.

KS-MemoryBench v1 brings together the three snapshot-history checkpoints, held-out forcing trajectories, and the two kinds of error tables. Its contents make the history-length comparison inspectable, but the description does not give any numerical errors or say which checkpoint performs best.
When I say 4-, 16-, and 64-snapshot checkpoints, am I describing three history-length variants?

Yes. Those labels distinguish latent SDE checkpoints by the number of observation snapshots used for their histories: 4, 16, or 64. In the associated fitting activity, the observations are eight Kuramoto–Sivashinsky Fourier modes. The artifact description does not specify the snapshots’ spacing or the time span of each history.
Does listing a checkpoint mean its predictions meet either accuracy target?

No. A checkpoint is a model artifact; its presence is not an accuracy finding. The tables contain normalized energy-W1 and mean-response errors, but no entries are stated here. We cannot infer from the inventory whether the stationary energy-distribution W1 is below 5% of the full-system distribution’s standard deviation or whether nonzero mean-energy responses to unseen weak forcing are within 10% relative error against full-system simulations.
What should a reader take ‘held-out forcing trajectories’ to mean?

They are trajectories associated with forcing held out for the response comparison, rather than a claim about a particular response result. The description does not say what forcing signals they use, how many trajectories there are, or whether the stored trajectories are full-system trajectories, reduced-model trajectories, or both.
Can I describe those trajectories as proof of generalization to unseen forcing?

Not on the basis of their presence alone. They provide material associated with held-out forcing, while response accuracy must be read from the relevant comparison. The artifact description does not state the measured errors or establish that a generalization target was met.
How are the normalized energy-W1 table and the mean-response error table different?

They report different kinds of discrepancy. Energy Wasserstein-1 concerns the distance between energy distributions, in this setting the stationary-energy comparison. Mean-response error concerns prediction of an energy response to forcing. Having both tables keeps those assessments distinct; a value in one would not automatically determine a value in the other.
Does ‘normalized energy-W1’ tell us the normalization denominator?

No. The artifact description says the energy-W1 values are normalized, but it does not define the normalization. The goal expresses its distributional threshold using the full-system stationary energy distribution’s standard deviation; we should not assume that this is the table’s denominator without an explicit definition.
Then can we read a table entry as a percentage of that standard deviation?

Not from this description alone. To interpret a normalized entry as that percentage, we would need to know that the entry divides W1 by the full-system distribution’s standard deviation. No such convention is specified for KS-MemoryBench v1 here.
Is the mean-response error table necessarily a table of relative errors?

The artifact calls it a mean-response error table without defining the error formula. The goal’s response criterion is relative error for nonzero mean-energy responses compared with full-system simulations, but the artifact description itself does not specify the table’s calculation or aggregation convention.
Does v1 imply there is an earlier benchmark whose results we should compare?
No. ‘v1’ is part of the artifact’s name. This description neither identifies another version nor supplies a comparison with one.
Should I say the benchmark includes the observed Fourier-mode data too?

Not unless that is stated separately. The associated activity fits the SDEs on eight observed KS Fourier modes, but the listed contents of KS-MemoryBench v1 are checkpoints, held-out forcing trajectories, and normalized energy-W1 and mean-response error tables. It does not explicitly list the observation data as a stored component.
What is the most precise way to describe what the artifact actually contains?

KS-MemoryBench v1 contains latent SDE checkpoints for 4-, 16-, and 64-snapshot histories, held-out forcing trajectories, and tables reporting normalized energy-Wasserstein-1 and mean-response errors. That states the artifact’s contents without assigning numerical values, defining an unstated normalization, or claiming that any accuracy target has been achieved.
I want to audit KS-MemoryBench v1 by comparing the 4-, 16-, and 64-snapshot held-out response errors against 10% and their normalized energy W1 values against 0.05.

That audit uses the benchmark’s error tables to assess both properties for each snapshot-history length. The held-out response errors are compared with 10%, and the normalized energy-Wasserstein-1 values are compared with 0.05. The audit is an activity to perform; no table entries or pass–fail outcomes are given here.
Should I make those comparisons separately for all three checkpoints?

Yes. The specified audit covers the 4-, 16-, and 64-snapshot variants. Comparing each variant’s held-out response error with 10% and its normalized energy W1 with 0.05 lets the two criteria be considered separately for each history length. The instructions do not indicate how any of the three compares.
Why keep the response and energy comparisons separate?

They assess different things. Held-out response error concerns predictions under forcing, whereas energy W1 concerns agreement between stationary energy distributions. A checkpoint’s comparison with one threshold does not determine its comparison with the other.
Is the 10% comparison relevant to the question about whether 16 snapshots capture hidden-mode memory?

Yes. The 16-snapshot hypothesis predicts less than 10% relative mean-energy response error under held-out weak forcing, as part of its claim that the history captures memory relevant to those responses. Auditing the 16-snapshot response error is therefore relevant to that prediction. The audit’s stated comparison, however, does not itself report an error or establish how the latent state represents hidden modes.
Does the 10% figure have exactly the same boundary in the hypothesis and in the broader goal?

The hypothesis says *less than* 10% relative error, which is a strict inequality. The broader goal says *within* 10% relative error for nonzero mean-energy responses to unseen weak forcing against full-system simulations. This audit says to compare errors against 10%; it does not report a value at the boundary or add a rule for classifying one.
Can any held-out forcing-response error in the table be treated automatically as a test of that specific hypothesis?

Not without checking what the entry represents. The hypothesis specifically concerns relative mean-energy response error under held-out weak forcing for the 16-snapshot history. The audit names held-out response errors, but its wording does not define their calculation, identify which forcing is weak, or specify snapshot spacing. Those distinctions matter if the comparison is used to assess the hypothesis precisely.
Does this audit tell us that the 16-snapshot checkpoint uses 0.25-time-unit spacing?

No. The 16-snapshot hypothesis specifies 0.25-time-unit spacing, but the audit identifies the checkpoint by snapshot count and does not state its spacing. The audit alone cannot establish that the checkpoint has the timing specified in the hypothesis.
What about the normalized energy W1 threshold of 0.05? Is that simply 5% written as a decimal?

It is the numerical threshold specified for the normalized energy-W1 comparison in this audit. The broader stationary-distribution goal requires an unnormalized Wasserstein-1 error below 5% of the full-system distribution’s standard deviation. The two thresholds have the same numerical form if the normalization divides W1 by that standard deviation, but KS-MemoryBench v1’s normalization has not been defined in the supplied description. I would not claim the two comparisons are equivalent without that definition.
So the audit can still say ‘compare normalized energy W1 against 0.05’?

Yes. That is exactly the specified audit comparison. It is distinct from asserting, without a stated normalization convention, that an entry below 0.05 necessarily establishes the broader Wasserstein-1 criterion.
